study.title: Numbers 24 - The blessing of Balaam and the announcements about the nations
study.overview: In this chapter, Balaam abandons the attempt to use agours and begins to speak under the direction of the Spirit of God. What would be a curse against Israel turns into blessing, and the message expands to include oracles about the future of Israel and the fate of neighboring peoples. The chapter highlights that God rules history, frustrating human intentions and preserving his people.

outline.title: Balaam Blesses Israel Moved by the Spirit
outline.explanation: Balaam realizes that the Lord desires to bless Israel and no longer seek agonists. Inspired by God, he describes the beauty, order, and prosperity of the people, as well as their future dominion over enemies. The blessing ends with the promise that those who bless Israel will be blessed and those who curse you will be cursed.

outline.title: The wrath of Balak and the farewell of Balaam
outline.explanation: Balak reacts with indignation because Balaam blessed Israel three times. He dispenses it without honor, and Balaam answers remembering that he could not speak by his own will against the word of the Lord. Even though, Balaam announces that he will still reveal what Israel will do to Moab in the future.

outline.title: The oracle of the scepter and the star
outline.explanation: Balaam speaks again, claiming to have heard the knowledge of the Most High. His prophecy announces a ruler associated with star and sceptre, image of real power, who will slay Moab and triumph over other enemies. The text also affirms Jacob's supremacy and the destruction of what remains of the opposition.

outline.title: Judgment on Amalek, the Tyranites and Other Poties
outline.explanation: Balaam uttereth oracles against Amalek, announcing his end, and against the Natives, who, though strong and secure, would be cast out and taken captive. Finally, he speaks of afflictions from Chitin against Assur and Eber, concluding that they will also perish, and then Balaam and Balak separate.

study.context: The chapter resumes the scene of confrontation between Balak king of Moab and Balaam, called to curse Israel. The notes indicate that Balaam already knew that the agourians could not harm the people of God and therefore fail to resort to divination practices. The text also mentions peoples and rulers such as Agague, Moab, Amalek, Aneus, Assur, Éber, and Chitin, but does not provide in the chapter itself additional historical details about them all. The sources observe that Balaam speaks as a prophet, even though his life and intentions remain ambiguous.
study.theology: The main theological emphasis is God's sovereignty: when he decides to bless, no human intent can reverse this decision. The Spirit of God can empower even a morally suspicious messenger to pronounce divine truth. The chapter also affirms God's faithfulness to Abraham's promise to bless those who bless his people and curse those who curse him. Moreover, the figure of the star and sceptre points to the hope of just and victorious government in Israel; evangelical readings can see there a historical reference to David and, more broadly, a figure that many Christians understand as fulfilled in Jesus, but this should be treated as an interpretation, not as an explicit statement of every detail of the text. The chapter ends by showing that the powers of the nations are also under the control of God.

scholarViews.insight: Balaam ceases to seek agouros and becomes directly inspired by the Spirit of God to pronounce the blessing upon Israel.
Balak's fury shows the total frustration of his attempt to turn blessing into a curse; the text emphasizes that Balaam could not speak against the Lord's will.

The expression about the star and the sceptre is understood as an image of real power, and Clarke notes that many relate it to Christ, although he recognizes the difficulty of fixing all the details of the prophecy.

questions: What does this chapter teach about the difference between human intentions and the sovereign will of God?
How does the star and scepter figure help think of the hope of a righteous king for Israel?
In what way does Balak's reaction expose the limit of any attempt to manipulate what God has already decided?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to trust that God rules even situations in which hostile people try to prevent his purpose. In practice, this leads us to abandon spiritual manipulations, divination and any attempt to control the future, and to seek fidelity to God's word. It also invites us to examine whether our words build or resist what God wants to do with his people. In times of opposition, concrete application is to pray with confidence, act with integrity and bless rather than to respond with revenge.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not unequivocally identify all the historical details of the mentioned peoples, nor does it fully explain the scope of terms such as star, sceptre, Quitim, Éber and the sons of Seth. The notes suggest interpretive possibilities, such as the relationship with David and, for some Christians, with Jesus, but these readings remain interpretations. There is also variation in the notes as to the exact nature of the agourians and the previous knowledge of Balaam.
